In 1987 the Southam survey found one in four Canadians to be functionally illiterate. These studies help reveal the magnitude of the illiteracy problem which challenges the future development of our country.
As we move to address this problem, our actions must be placed in a larger context. Illiteracy is just one part of the puzzle. Our actions on literacy therefore must be part of a much broader strategy to improve social mobilization and our social welfare system.
Our efforts must be accompanied by actions in areas like training, education, child care, employment equity, and initiatives to address the problem of poverty in this country.

speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider means of ensuring that regional development remains a priority in all decisions to be made by the government.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I am delighted to have the opportunity today to debate my motion on regional development. I know that this question has been addressed in the past on numerous occasions, but it seems
that it will have to be debated over and over again for the regions of this country actually to see any benefits.
It is especially important now because the regions of this country feel a sense of alienation like never before. Whether it is in western Canada, in the north, in northern Ontario, in northern or eastern Quebec or in Atlantic Canada, these regions have one thing in common. They feel that their government in Ottawa has forgotten about them, and they feel that Ottawa does not care. This is a tragedy.
This is what is slowly killing the heart of our country. Whatever I can do to contribute to reversing this disastrous trend, I will gladly do. This situation has become particularly critical with the Conservative administration.
This government, as we all know, is running the country like a corporation, putting principles like corporate profits and good balance sheets ahead of the interests of people. It is not even doing that well.
As Atlantic Canadians have always known, when the national government operates purely on economic efficiency principles the regions are bound to suffer. The centrepiece, the raison d'etre of the Conservative government's two mandates, is the so-called free trade agreement. With this agreement, Canada is now in a position where it cannot make regional development a priority. It cannot do that because the FTA is basically a bill of rights for the corporate giants, and their objectives become the priorities of this government without questioning.
What the corporate giants basically want, besides free access to our natural resources, is the creation of a level playing field which would use the American standard as a model. Therefore, on behalf of corporate America, the Conservative government is presently well on its way to changing Canadian standards to bring them down to those of the U.S.
This means that our social programs are being destroyed one by one and that anything considered a subsidy by corporate America is being dismantled. The federal government's financial involvement in creating

the circumstances which will enhance regional development is considered a subsidy by corporate America.
Even though the Prime Minister had vowed that free trade would not hurt the regions and that regional equality would be one of the benefits of the deal, there is convincing evidence that his heartless, big business oriented agenda is a betrayal of the Canadian concept of regional equality.
I would like to summarize the main consequences of this so-called free trade agreement on Atlantic Canada. When most of the country was well out of the 1982 recession, Atlantic Canada was still struggling. Instead of helping our region, the present government has made it worse. Many Atlantic Canadians believe that this situation is the result of vengeance by the Tory government and the Prime Minister, in particular, toward the citizens of this country who had the foresight to vote Liberal in the last election. Something that has really put our development in jeopardy has been the dismantling of our transportation system.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport

speechtext: Can you say that with a straight face?

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS - MOTIONS   REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT GOVERNMENT PRIORITY
speechtext:
Yes, with a very straight face, and I could wipe the grin off yours too, maybe before this is over.
Privatization, deregulation and cuts in subsidies have sadly diminished our ability to transport people and goods in and out of Atlantic Canada, creating a situation where continuing development becomes extremely difficult.
The air transport companies are now in private hands. They operate wherever they choose, which is where the bigger profits are, and as a consequence smaller communities are losing an essential means of transportation or are left with second-class service. And the worst is yet to come.
Rail transportation is also under attack. We have witnessed the decimation of VIA Rail. On top of losing 447 jobs, maritimers now have only one Atlantic train, a combination of the Ocean and the Atlantic, from Halifax to Montreal six times weekly. We also lost the Halifax-Yarmouth run, the Halifax-Sydney, the Halifax-Port Hawkesbury, the Moncton-Campbellton-Edmunston, the Halifax-Moncton-Saint John routes. Moreover, we
lost a bus route on to Prince Edward Island that links the province to VIA at Moncton.
By failing to promote an efficient rail transportation system the Tories are putting additional pressure on our roads, which will need major improvements since more truck traffic is evident on all of the highways in this country. The subsidies to railways for moving export grain and flour to eastern ports were also cancelled. The Atlantic Provinces Transportation Commission estimates that $14.4 million in activity will be lost to the region because of the termination of the At and East program. Should both Atlantic grain elevators be unable to continue their operations, which is likely, the resulting negative impact would be somewhere in the vicinity of $34.3 million.
The decision made by this government following the free trade agreement has resulted in the crippling of our transportation system which needed improvement and without which sustainable development for our region becomes impossible.
One good idea that this government has put in place, I must say, is ACOA. The good thing about this agency was that it was set up in the region. It was staffed by people of the region, and these people were making decisions on something that they knew.
Originally, the ACOA budget was $1.05 billion for five years, an humble investment but an investment nevertheless. The problem is that the Tory government found a way to turn a good thing into a bad one. The Prime Minister has a real talent for that.
With its incentive right wing agenda, it decided to spread the amount over seven years instead of five, which means a cut of 28 per cent. One of the consequences of these cuts is that ACOA officials have to deal with too many cases at the same time, which does not permit the proper counselling to allow success to happen as quickly as it should. People are becoming more and disillusioned with the program and are losing faith, which is a sad commentary on this government's record.
The Conservative government has also signed co-operation agreements with the Atlantic provinces. The agreements replace the economic regional development agreements that were put in place by the Liberal government. The result for Atlantic Canada is a loss of more than $300 million. We could surely use that amount of development in these tough times. We need it badly
December 17, 1990

to build an economic structure without which we will never be able to contribute positively to the wealth of the country.
The Conservative government is also cutting transfer payments to the Atlantic Canada. This means cuts to medicare and post-secondary education, which is totally unacceptable. There has been $17.7 million cut this year and $37 million will be cut next year. This is what Tories call progress.
On top of that, with its fiscal and monetary policies designed to suppress inflation concentrated in southern Ontario by high interest rates and an artificially high dollar which again come directly from the free trade deal, the Tory government has been killing jobs at an alarming pace in Atlantic Canada and in the rest of the country.
This is without mentioning the closing down of rural post offices, the cuts to CBC, to Radio-Canada, the mismanagement of the fisheries, and the delay in the Hibernia project.
Once the table is set for an economic and social disaster, what does the government do? It cuts our unemployment insurance program. Approximately 77,500 Atlantic Canadians will see a net loss in UI benefits this year. This could not have come at a worse time. Unemployment insurance has always been seen as a means for the federal government to achieve rough equality across the country and buffer sections of the regions experiencing hardship.
What is totally unacceptable once again is that corporate America believes our federal government's support of the UI program constitutes a subsidy and therefore presents an unfair advantage to Canadian companies and employers. The Tory government decided to lower our standards to U.S. levels. Now the total cost of the program will be borne by employees and employers and those who will suffer are the people and the regions of this country. Atlantic Canada will be especially hard hit.
I could go on talking about the mess which the Tory government, acting on behalf of the interests of corporate America, has inflicted on Atlantic Canada. What we have to do now is think of solutions. Are there any? I believe there are. Yes, there is a solution but only if there is political will.

Let us take a quick look at what the parties are offering as solutions. There seems to be a consensus that an effective regional development polity is vital for Canada. Unfortunately, however, no one seems to agree on how to accomplish this goal, primarily because no one seems to agree on what an effective regional development polity should be.
Let us take a look at the views that have been expressed in this House. I am convinced, Mr. Speaker, that examination of the varying approaches to regional development will reveal the strength of the Liberal Party's perspective.
The NDP has made it clear that it disagrees with current government policy on regional development. It is argued that we should go back to the way things were, when we had the Department of Regional Economic Expansion. It is argued that we must have a holistic approach to regional development. In order to develop such an approach, the NDP calls for the creation of a standing committee and a specific government department to deal with regional development. This department's mandate would cover the whole gambit of economic development in a certain region. For example, transportation, fisheries and economic development would be looked at as a whole rather than in isolation.
On this basis, the NDP has expressed its dissatisfaction with the government's decentralized approach to regional development. The creation of ACOA, for example, has been criticized. It is argued that its power and its mandate are far too limited and that the interests of Atlantic Canada would perhaps best be served if there was a department set up in Ottawa.
The Conservatives, on the other hand, defend their policies by saying that ACOA is effective precisely because it is centred in Atlantic Canada where Atlantic Canadians can play a leading role in determining what it does and how it functions. Moreover, they point out that even though the ACOA headquarters is located in Moncton, there are regional offices in each of the provincial capitals as well as Ottawa.
There are valid points made by both the New Democrats and even by the Conservatives. However, there are numerous misleading and, permit me to say, false statements as well. The view of the Liberal Party is based on a combination of the valid points and the elimination of the false ones. The NDP approach to regional development is regressive. The Conservative approach is corpo-ratist. There seems to be a consensus that an effective regional development policy is vital for Canada. Un-

The Liberals believe that if Canada is to be competitive, it is essential that regional development policies and public investment decisions be a fundamental part of national economic policy. We believe that this country needs the advantages to be gained from strong regional economies.
We believe that economic growth in the next two decades will be highly focused on knowledge and service-based activities. Industries will depend for their success upon an educated and productive labour force and upon cost-effective communications systems for the transfer of data and new knowledge. There will be no need to restrict these industries to the industrial heartland of Canada. Quality of life, communication services, personal transportation and information processing facilities will be dominant factors in determining where business in the future prospers.
We believe that the Canadian government can create the conditions that can attract knowledge-based and resource-based industries to slow growth areas of Canada, such as Atlantic Canada. In other words, we believe that it is possible to do the opposite of what is being done today by this Tory government.
Well-planned public investments can stimulate private sector investments. We want to direct public investment to slow growth areas. Atlantic Canada, in particular, still requires strong investment to develop further its basic infrastructure. We believe, Mr. Speaker, that the Canadian government not only can intervene, but must intervene to achieve that end which will enable Atlantic Canada to eventually become a contributor to our national wealth.

speakeroldname: Mr. Andre Plourde (Parliamentary Secretaiy to Minister of Industry, Science and Technology):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS - MOTIONS   REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT GOVERNMENT PRIORITY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the global economy has embraced a rapidly changing new order in recent years. Industrially and commercially, the essential characteristic of this new order is market globalization or the internationalization of business. For an extremely large and underpopulated country such as ours, this presents a number of challenges which are basic to the preservation of our standard of living, our social programs and our systems of values.
For Canada, and for Quebec in particular, this wave of economic change, although risky, presents novel opportunities for development and prosperity which should be explored.
In the last six years, our economic actions have been predicated entirely upon one fundamental goal: to ensure that all regions of Canada benefit from the emerging new economic order. From the start, we devised a long-range action plan that would enable us to reach this objective.
The problems of Quebec are related to a number of phenomena, such as the emergence of a new industrial order, market globalization, the increased role of competition in international trade and the increasingly vital roles played by research, development and staff training in opening up and maintaining markets. It is essential that these data be taken into account in any regional development policy.
Mr Speaker, for six years now, Quebec has recorded steady economic growth that has allowed it to make strides in the modernization of its industrial base. A good deal still remains to be done, however, before this modernization is completed.
Regional development problems in Quebec, moreover, must take into account one fundamental fact, namely, the dual nature of Quebec's economy. On the one hand, the central regions of the province consist essentially in urban areas comprising 85 percent of the province's population; the economies of these regions are centred on the secondary and tertiary sectors. On the other hand, the resource regions of Quebec cover more

than 90 percent of the province's territory, yet are home to less than 15 percent of the population. The economy of these resource regions is centred essentially on the primary sector and the exploitation of natural resources such as forest, mineral and fisheries resources.
Mr. Speaker, we signed with the Quebec government a master agreement on regional development which takes into account this duality and the different needs of the central and resource regions of Quebec. Let us take a closer look at the different needs of these regions.
In the central regions, such as greater Montreal, the Quebec City region, the Eastern Townships, the Bois-Francs region and the Outaouais, the economy is more diversified and more developed. Traditional sectors remain active here, but they have been eclipsed in importance by new sectors. We must now accelerate the modernization of production facilities and take steps to ensure that companies swiftly incorporate advanced technologies that will make them more productive, efficient and competitive in order that they may carve out market niches for themselves.
It is clear, in this context, that the economy of the greater Montreal region faces a number of special needs. Because this region is in direct competition with other major North American cities, and nearly half the population of Quebec resides within its boundaries, the economy of the Montreal region has a direct influence on the development of other regions in the province. It is therefore essential that the establishment and maintenance of modem economic sectors be stimulated in this region, since such sectors generate sustainable, quality jobs as well as considerable activity in other related sectors.
In recent years, the Montreal region has made significant advances in dynamic and forward-looking sectors. Aeronautics, for example, is strongly represented in the region by companies such as Bombardier, Pratt & Whitney, Bell Helicopter as well as Spar Aerospace, which has been commissioned to build RADARSAT, the first remote sensing satellite to be designed and built entirely in Canada. The decision to locate the Canadian Space Agency within the region, on the south shore of the St. Lawrence, will undoubtedly help to generate considerable local economic activity in the fields of aeronautics and telecommunications.

Montreal also developed a network a big and small businesses specialized in microelectronics, informatics, software development and the manufacture of printed circuits.
Other job-producing economic sectors have maintained their presence in the greater Montreal region. These include pharmaceuticals, biotechnology and consulting engineering (with such giants as Lavallin and SNC).
All of these sectors require advanced technologies and considerable value added. They provide quality jobs, and their export potential is high. It is vital that the Montreal economy rely more and more on these forward-looking sectors.
Of course, the various levels of government are prepared to do their share, set up programs and coordinate efforts in this direction. It is nevertheless clear that business must make an immediate commitment to the research and development inherent in economic development.
It is all the more essential, Mr. Speaker, that we devote efforts to our resource regions, considering that their industrial base lacks diversification and is often threatened, that these regions are located far away from major urban centres and that unemployment is definitely higher in these regions than in urban areas.
Initiatives have therefore been taken to turn our natural resources to good account by enhancing management and conservation with a view to sustainable development. The technical and professional skills of labour must also be improved.
For example, in the logging, pulp and paper and lumber industries, we are working with the Quebec government for the improvement of timber management, the construction of new access roads to these resources and above all reforestation, which is essential to sustainable development.
We also allocated funds for the diversification of regional enterprises, and for development programs in the agri-food and agriculture sectors.
In response to the need for modernization of production equipment we have set up a series of programs. Thus, the federal government's concerted Enterprise Development Program and Manufacturing Productivity Improvement Program are designed specifically to sup-

December 17, 1990
Private Members' Business
port small businesses engaging in equipment modernization and industrial diversification projects.
Mr. Speaker, in closing, it is most essential that everyone understand the challenges and the development possibilities involved, that objectives be mutually agreed upon and that everyone work towards the same end. For its part, the government will continue to allocate resources as judiciously as possible, and will also continue to inform Quebec businesses about how best to benefit from the free trade agreement between Canada and the United States.

Mr. Speaker, it is certainly a pleasure to speak to the motion of my colleague from Miramichi on regional development.
I commend my colleague, the hon. member for Miramichi, for his motion and for keeping the issue of regional development alive. In his region and in mine, a continued strong federal presence and commitment to economic development is critical. In the north, we have seen, over the past couple of years, a declining commitment.
For example, the federal government has cut back its fiscal transfers to the Yukon and Northwest Territories. In 1984, the previous Liberal government had negotiated five-year formula funding agreements with the two territorial governments.
In the renegotiation of these agreements last year, the current federal government changed that formula. It reduced it so the two territories will receive less funding over the next five years than they would have received under the original formula. Specifically, the Northwest Territories will receive about $110 million less over the next five years. The Yukon government will receive about $80 million less.
In addition to these cutbacks, both territories are still waiting for renewal of the northern economic development agreements. They are now in the process of
negotiations. I hope the government of the Northwest Territories will be successful in coming to a conclusion that is preferable for the Northwest Territories.
In 1984, the Yukon and the federal government signed a five-year economic development agreement worth $26.4 million. That general agreement and the subsidiary agreements negotiated under it, expired in March 1989. Almost two years later, we still do not have a new economic development agreement with the Yukon. It is true that the federal government has provided some interim funding to the Yukon government to cany on some activities, but not all the previously funded components received interim funding.
In the Northwest Territories, the picture is similar. In 1987, a four-year economic development agreement worth $38.3 million was signed. Two of the six subsidiaiy agreements negotiated under that general agreement expired last March. One of them, the tourism sub-agreement, received some interim funding.
The other four sub-agreements expire this coming March. For both of the territories, renewed economic development agreements are necessary for territorial economic growth.
In the Northwest Territories, the government is looking for a more flexible program which can be utilized in less developed areas and communities and which has less emphasis on profitability. We are anxiously awaiting announcements from the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development concerning renewed economic development agreements with both territories and we will be looking, as well, for adequate funding in these agreements.
The north continues to be extremely concerned about the effects of the goods and services tax on both northern consumers and businesses. With the highest cost of living in the country, the goods and services tax is going to affect the northern territories more adversely than anywhere else. I say this especially for the eastern Arctic, the area that I represent, where the cost of living in the area can be about two and a half times higher than that in the city of Ottawa. A litre of milk might cost $5 compared to $1 and some cents for a litre of milk in Ottawa. So, Mr. Speaker, I think we have to convince
December 17, 1990

this government that it has to do as much as it can for regional and northern development.
For the past couple of years, I and other northerners have been telling the finance minister that the GST is going to do us more harm than good. The finance minister stubbornly continues to insist that we will benefit, despite evidence to the contrary. The finance minister maintains that the north will be better off with the goods and services tax. I can point out that resource development might be better off-I say "might" with a question mark-under the GST, but the average person living in Pond Inlet, Coppermine, Pelly Bay or Grise Fiord will not be better off because the purchasing power of that individual will be a lot less and certainly the purchasing power for groceries will be a lot less because of having to pay 7 per cent tax on other goods which presently are not taxed under the MST.
The most recent confirmation of the negative impact of the GST on the north has been pointed out in a report by Ernst and Young, management consultants. This report was made public earlier this month by the Ontario government. It is a report that was commissioned by the provincial and territorial ministers responsible for economic development in the north. I will quote a few excerpts from this report for the benefit of hon. members and for anyone from the finance minister's office who may be listening.
As it is typical of the minister, in replying to my question on this issue in the House a couple of weeks ago, he picked out the only positive aspect of this report and quoted it verbatim to the House when I asked him a question about this report. On the negative side, I quote: "Small business, in all sectors, will be hit by high compliance costs which will be particularly onerous in the north, due to the lack of professional advisory services".
Arts and crafts is an important industry to the residents of the eastern Arctic. This report says that these activities, and I quote: "-will be negatively affected by the goods and services tax, since original works of art have been exempt from the FST but will be subject to the GST. The cost of transporting the art to southern markets will also bear GST, even where the artist can select to be exempt, as a result of having sales of less than $30,000 per year".
Private Members' Business
I would just like to read one more quote: "Municipalities, universities, hospitals and schools in the north will bear higher over all costs under the GST. Rebates for these institutions are to be based on a single national calculation of the increase in the tax burden associated with sales tax reform. However, because local mark-ups and transport costs did not bear FST, the FST content of institutional purchase in the north had been lower than in the south. The rebates will therefore not be sufficient to compensate for the additional tax burden under the GST. "
I would like to take this opportunity to support the motion of my colleague for Miramichi on regional development.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS - MOTIONS   REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT GOVERNMENT PRIORITY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to have the opportunity to participate today and say a few words with regard to regional development. It is a priority of this government. The results are coming through loud and clear.
I also want to say a few words with regard to the Western Diversification Fund that was announced in 1987. The act was passed in 1988, allocating $1.2 billion to the four western provinces. The head office is in Edmonton, but there are satellite offices within each province.
The government has adopted a regional approach that reflects the special circumstances, the needs, the uniqueness, the strength and even indeed the weaknesses of certain areas.
Western Canadians know that we live with a very volatile resource base where oil, gas and agriculture unfortunately are not stable commodities but tend to have peaks and valleys. The Western Diversification program has been extremely successful. It is one that I have worked with quite a bit.
Over 1,866 regular projects have been approved, representing about $542 million since inception. I also want to say that the assistance is not being used to bail out or shore up businesses that are in trouble. It is not used to modernize plants nor expand existing businesses, but it works to promote diversification. That was its main policy in the form of new products, new technologies, new techniques, new markets and import replacements for western Canada.
They have also supported 16 systemic projects representing about $52 million. One that I would like to refer to is the Centre for Frontier Engineering Research,

CFER. It has just sent out a special issue with regard to the opening of its project. It was an $18 million project in Edmonton la st May 28.
This certainly shows co-operation where the federal government worked in co-operation with the provincial government and private enterprise to see this become a reality.
I feel not only has this been extremely beneficial but the other aspect about WD is that 80 per cent of the commitments are repayable. WD gives a helping hand. It gives people a kick-start. We do not have hand-out programs.
The other thing that was interesting in the Speech from the Throne in 1989 was the government's procurement policy. They were told to direct themselves toward regional considerations. In the last couple of years western Canada has received three or four major contracts. One had to do with the Department of Transport's CAATS contract for $380 million. It was awarded to Hughes Aircraft Canada which will open offices in Calgary and Vancouver. The contract was $380 million with spin-offs of over $500 million across Canada.
Also, there was a contract awarded to Computing Devices Canada for over $1 billion from the Department of National Defence. These people are going to open a head office in Calgary. Eighty per cent of that $1 billion will certainly go into the western part of Canada.
In conclusion, I have to say that the ACOA head office in Moncton with $1.05 billion, FEDNOR headquartered in Sault Ste. Marie with $60 million over five years and Western Diversification with the $1.2 billion, have certainly served to diversify. No longer do people sitting in Ottawa make the decisions. It is people in the regions making decisions for the regions and their needs. Diversification is very important.
We are always open to amendments, to improvement, and to ways to do the job better. This is one area that has really been successful. The motion being discussed today is really a non-starter. We are in there. We are doing it. Regional diversification is a priority with this government and always will be.

Mr. Speaker, on Friday the B.C. Central Credit Union published a report outlining the foreign control of our forest industry. The report's results are of serious concern. Foreign corporations now control just over 43 per cent of industry assets according to this study.

TRIBUTE TO THE LATE MGR. ALBERTUS MARTIN
speechtext:
With the passing of Monsignor Albertus Martin, Mr. Speaker, the people of the Nicolet diocese and the rest of Quebec certainly have lost one of the greatest builders and defenders of the Church in Quebec.
Monsignor Martin was a scholar and a world-class canon law specialist. He had been thoroughly involved in the reforms suggested by Vatican II. He was endowed with a remarkable intelligence and was recognized as a man of exceptional apostolic dedication. His administrative and leadership skills led him to found the Nicolet Seminary, rebuild the Nicolet cathedral following its destruction and give a sound financial basis to each of those parishes.
A very accessible man, he knew how to round up his flock following a disaster, whether a fire, a death, a sickness or the loss of a job. He left behind him apostolic accomplishments beyond compare. His simplicty, dedication, hard work, honesty, generosity, kindness and class made him really a man of God.
Monsignor Martin used to quote St. Paul often. Thinking of him, I wish to quote St. Paul. In his Epistle to the Galatians, he wrote: "But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness, faith, meekness and temperance". This certainly describes perfectly Monsignor Martin's heritage. Monsignor Martin, farewell and thank you!

SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in its report last week the Standing Committee on Industry, Science and Technology of the House of
Commons made the simple statement that the economic well-being of Canadians depended on science and technology.
If we want jobs in Canada we have to add value to products and services through science and technology and the skills of Canadians, not just scientists and technologists but the men and women who work on the shop floor across this country.
This is a simple message which to now has not been understood by the Conservative government. A newspaper headline on the weekend read: "PM Shatters Dreams of Top Canadian Scientists". The headline is wrong. It should read: "PM Shatters Dreams of all Canadians".
This government has damaged Canada's R and D capacity, cut support for industrial research and development, cut transfer payments for post-secondary education, and cut funds for training.
Can we hope for a death-bed conversion from this government, or is it too late to reverse a disastrous record?

speakerposition: subtopic
subtopic: NATIVE HOUSING
NATIVE HOUSING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is now the holiday season and it is incumbent upon us to promote the spirit of giving and caring for our brothers and sisters. Yet it is a tragic fact that many of our nation's first peoples live in overcrowded homes, often without water and sewage facilities.
Can aboriginal children receive the education they need when they return each night to a crowded house? Can they return to school fresh and ready to learn after trying to sleep with many others in these same rooms? Can seniors expect to retain good health? Can expectant mothers hope to provide proper care in such conditions?
This is a good time for the government to make its New Year's resolution to the native peoples of Canada. This government must commit itself to alleviating the problem of substandard housing.
For many natives housing has improved, but not for all. I think it only fitting that we in this House do what we can to help the native people improve housing conditions in their communities.

SKI NORQUAY

IMMIGRATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on August 31 of this year, the Minister of Employment and Immigration eliminated the self-exile category for east Europeans wishing to immigrate to Canada.
At the same time the minister imposed a 40 per cent slowdown in the processing of these applications already in the system. The result has been a three to four-year delay for the outcome of these applications. The delay is causing a financial burden on government and undue hardship on applicants and Canadian sponsors.
I would like to urge the minister, first, to lift all the restrictions for the final disposition for Canadian consulates; second, remove the 40 per cent slowdown of processing; third, give high priority to all self-exile applications; and, fourth, allow work permit authorizations for those applicants already in Canada awaiting the final decision.
These proposed changes will not create a need for a change in regulations, only a change in policy, which is firmly in the minister's power.
In the spirit of Christmas, I ask the minister to implement these four recommendations before the House rises for the winter break.

speakerposition: subtopic
subtopic: THE LATE CARL NICKLE
THE LATE CARL NICKLE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to pay tribute to a former member of this House, Mr. Carl Nickle, who passed away in Calgary last week at the age of 76.
Carl Nickle served as the member of Parliament for the ridings of Calgary West and Calgary South respectively from 1951 to 1957, using this place as a forum to promote the interests of western Canada passionately.
The son of oilman Sam Nickle, Carl was raised and educated in Calgary where he founded both the Daily Oil Bulletin and the Canadian Oil Register before going on to establish his own oil company, Conventures Ltd.
Nickle's achievements were certainly not confined to the oil industry. He served with the Canadian army from 1939 to 1948 where he achieved the rank of lieutenant. An avid coin collector, he became a prominent philanthropist, underwriting the Nickle Art Museum at the University of Calgary and playing a key role in the creation of the Nickle family foundation, which provides scholarships to students and cultural groups.
Carl Nickle was an exceptional parliamentarian, a distinguished Canadian, and a friend.
To his wife, Diana, and their family, I extend sincere condolences.

FORESTRY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as chairman of the House of Commons subcommittee on forestry, I was very pleased today to receive a positive response to our recent report from a large group of national organizations that both individually and collectively expressed their interest in and their support for both the economic and the environmental interests in our forests as expressed by that report.
These organizations included the Canadian Forestry Association, the Canadian Institute of Forestry, the Canadian Pulp and Paper Association, the Canadian Federation of Woodlot Owners, the Canadian Wildlife Federation, Wildlife Habitat Canada, the Canadian Nature Federation, Ducks Unlimited Canada, and the Canadian Federation of Professional Foresters.

speakerposition: subtopic
subtopic: CPR TRAINING
CPR TRAINING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last Saturday evening a Canadian Airlines plane travelling from Ottawa to Vancouver was forced to make an emergency landing in Calgary. While on board, the 10-month old son of my constituents, Robert and Taunia Myrah, had stopped breathing. The flight attendants who were untrained in the procedures of cardiopulmonary resuscitation administered this technique while reading from a manual.
Because emergency medical assistance is not readily available while planes are in the air, it is inconceivable that flight personnel are not required to possess these life saving techniques.

The airlines must assure their passengers that at least one of their flight attendants is trained in these techniques should an emergency come up.

I offer my sincere condolences to the family of Colton Myrah and recommend that as many Canadians as possible become familiar with the life saving techniques of CPR.

subtopic: CANADA'S GREEN PLAN

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: CANADA'S GREEN PLAN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the residents of Fraser Valley East are very concerned with environmental issues. The beauty of the valley is often cloaked by ugly clouds of smog blown in from Vancouver. Air quality is not simply a cosmetic concern for the residents of Chilliwack, nor for that matter is the murkiness of the Fraser River a cosmetic concern. Every time we breathe the air or look at the water we are reminded of the pressing need for action.
The green plan for a healthy environment is a plan for action. I have made the minister aware of our concerns. The minister has listened, the minister has considered, and the minister has acted.
Targets are set for the establishment of comprehensive emission controls complete with a monitoring and advisory component. In 1991, the federal government will join with the Government of British Columbia to start development of a Fraser River action plan for the Fraser River and Burrard Inlet. The action plan will focus on restoring the river's fish population meaning clearer and cleaner water.
The green plan will ensure that the fresh is put back into fresh air and that the clean will be put back into clean water. This is definitely good news for residents of the Fraser Valley and indeed all Canadians.

subtopic: ILLITERACY

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
subtopic: ILLITERACY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, let us consider the following: in May a Statistics Canada report revealed that the reading skills of 2.9 million Canadians were too limited to allow them to deal with most of the written material they encounter in everyday life. In 1987 the Southam survey found one in four Canadians to be functionally illiterate. These studies help reveal the magnitude of the illiteracy problem which challenges the future development of our country.
As we move to address this problem, our actions must be placed in a larger context. Illiteracy is just one part of the puzzle. Our actions on literacy therefore must be part of a much broader strategy to improve social mobilization and our social welfare system.
Our efforts must be accompanied by actions in areas like training, education, child care, employment equity, and initiatives to address the problem of poverty in this country.
I look forward to our government moving forward on this social policy agenda. Yet at the same time I urge that this be done in a consistent, comprehensive and co-ordinated manner.

I have a question for him because he and his government did promise all workers that there would be recycling programs, but there is none. Is he now prepared to assure the Canadian people that there will not be further negotiations until such time as programs have been implemented to find work for the men and women who have been laid off as a result of the free trade policy of this government.

speakeroldname: Hon. Benoit Bouchard (Minister of Industry, Science and Technology):
speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
subtopic: INDUSTRY

December 17, 1990

has nothing to do with current job losses in Canada. These references to the economic recession-
Again, Mr. Speaker, I would suggest that Quebec labour was in favour of the free trade agreement, and Quebec remains supportive of this deal. Mr. Speaker, after the Liberal Party's lengthy filibuster over Bill C-21, my colleague the Minister of Employment and Immigration finally has the mechanisms she needs to provide Quebec workers with the recycling programs they want.
But as usual my colleague speaks from both sides of her mouth. At the time she should have done everything to help the House adopt the bill designed to help Quebec employers and workers, and things would have been much easier all around, Mr. Speaker.

speakerposition: subtopic
subtopic: FISHERIES
FISHERIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans. Last Friday the minister released a new Atlantic management plan that will apply for three years rather than the usual one. Part of that plan includes the introduction of individual boat quotas for the Scotia-Fundy inshore, a system which may cost many fishermen and communities their livelihood if it is put into place.
I ask the minister this. Why is he going to a three-year plan in the Scotia-Fundy area without first doing a comprehensive stock evaluation, as asked for by the fishing people in the area?

speakeroldname: Hon. Bernard Valcourt (Minister of Fisheries and Oceans):
speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
subtopic: FISHERIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the question of the hon. member as to the reason why we have introduced a three-year TAC in Scotia-Fundy is the same reason that we have done it for other parts of the Atlantic region. We are trying to build some stability in that fishery. What the fishermen, what the producers and what the manufacturers have told us is if they could get a longer term view of the fishery, they can do better planning, they can do better marketing. That is the reason why we have gone for this three-year TAC, by putting in the window, that is not carved in stone. If we get biological evidence or scientific evidence that the stock is on the verge of
collapse or that it is doing much better, then at that time we shall revise the TACs.

subtopic: FISHERIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the minister for his answer. I am sure if he spoke to the industry in the southern end of Nova Scotia, he would know that they would like to have a new evaluation.
My further question concerns the Minister of the Environment's green plan, which was introduced last week. I am sure the Minister of Fisheries is well aware that at page 76 it states:
Accordingly, in consultation with the fishing industry and the
provinces, the Government will put in place a system of Individual
Transferable Quotas (ITQs) for various fisheries.
I ask the minister, is this now polity? If so, what fisheries does he plan to privatize further on the east coast?

speakeroldname: Hon. Bernard Valcourt (Minister of Fisheries and Oceans):
speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
subtopic: FISHERIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am struck by that question, privatize. I did not know that the governments of Canada or Nova Scotia, for that matter, or any other were fishing. This belongs to the private sector. I tell the member that these fishermen are entrepreneurs. They are the ones who are harvesting the fish in the Atlantic Ocean.
When she asks me whether this is the policy, she should be aware that the draggermen of her area are the ones to whom we have offered to introduce these Individual Transferable Quotas. They are being implemented right now. They have been asking for it. She should listen to those fishermen more.

subtopic: FISHERIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Acting Prime Minister. The Minister for International Trade is now in Washington talking to U.S. and Mexican representatives regarding trade talks on a U.S.-Canada trade deal with Mexico. From reports, the United States has given Canada until February 1, 1991 to decide whether we will participate. The last time the United States gave Canada an ultimatum we lost 226,000 jobs in just two years of the U.S. trade deal.
I want to ask the government this: what is the response of this government to the latest U.S. ultimatum, yes or no?

speakeroldname: Hon. Tom Hockin (Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
subtopic: FISHERIES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, as I think the hon. member knows, the trade minister is meeting with the United States trade representative and the Mexican representative today. They will be making a decision shortly. By the end of January or early February the three governments should be in a position to announce what the shape of those negotiations will be. I hope these negotiations will help to increase the creation of jobs in Canada just as we have had since December, 1988, with 207,000 jobs created in Canada since the free trade agreement.

subtopic: FISHERIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, trade deals for Canada based on hope have certainly not proven in the interest of Canadian workers. Two hundred and twenty-six thousand who have lost their jobs know that.
My supplementary is for the minister. This government, despite the job losses, despite the loss to Canadian sovereignty, continues on the same old way of dragging Canada into something and it cannot even prove that the Canada-U.S. trade agreement has been good for Canada. All other statistics say it has not. Yet this government is now considering a deal with Mexico.
Before even considering being a part of these talks, will the minister undertake on behalf of his government a full public assessment of the results of the Canada-U.S. trade deal before getting us into another one?

speakeroldname: Hon. Tom Hockin (Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
subtopic: FISHERIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is very interesting when a spokesman from that side of the House and from the Liberal Party speak about the trade agreement. They always refer to one section of any country's trade balance and that is the manufacturing sector.
The manufacturing sector of Canada, the manufacturing sector of the United States, the manufacturing sector of Europe, the manufacturing sector of Japan have been declining in relationship to services for the past 20 years. There is nothing new about this. The manufacturing sector is declining.
What is not happening in other countries, and is happening in Canada, is that investment intentions in Canada, investment intentions in capital equipment,
Oral Questions
investment intentions in plant and equipment, hit record highs last year and they are up this year, 1990, 9.7 per cent over the previous year.

Last Friday in the management plan announced by the minister he included references to the dockside monitoring program that fishermen want no part of. According to fisheries officials, the program is to be fishermen funded and run by a third party contractor.
Is the minister having this program contracted out to avoid the heat from annoyed fishermen in Prince Edward Island?

The reason we are introducing a dockside monitoring program-

subtopic: FISHERIES
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subtopic: FISHERIES

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: FISHERIES

A good Liberal.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries and Oceans

If the hon. member cares so much for the fishermen, he should endorse the groundfish management plan because it is one that will ensure the conservation of these stocks for present fishermen and the next generation of fishermen in all of Atlantic Canada.

PERSIAN GULF
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is to the Acting Prime Minister. UN Resolution 678 authorizes member states to use force in the gulf after January 15. Talks before that date between Washington and Baghdad are currently non-existent.
Is Canada taking steps today to ensure that the UN Security Council is sponsoring its own peace negotiations before January 15?

speakeroldname: Hon. Mary Collins (Associate Minister of National Defence and Minister responsible for Status of Women):
speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Associate Minister of National Defence
subtopic: PERSIAN GULF
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I know that the Secretary of State for External Affairs is meeting with the NATO foreign ministers today and will be discussing the issue of the gulf.
Certainly it is our position that we would urge Saddam Hussein to quickly come to an agreement on a date to proceed with those meetings which would offer the best prospects for development of a peaceful resolution of this problem in the Middle East.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs has certainly been using his good offices to encourage and urge that these meetings take place as quickly as possible so that there be a possibility of a peaceful resolution.

subtopic: PERSIAN GULF
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is to the same minister. On Friday, President Bush referred to January 15 as the deadline for Iraq to withdraw from Kuwait.
I would like to repeat a question put to this House before but to which we have as yet an unsatisfactory response. Will the government assure us today that Canadian forces will not participate in any offensive action in the gulf before debate on the issue takes place in the House of Commons?

speakeroldname: Hon. Mary Collins (Associate Minister of National Defence and Minister responsible for Status of Women):
speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Associate Minister of National Defence
subtopic: PERSIAN GULF
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think this issue was thoroughly debated during the last debate that we had with respect to the UN Resolution. Obviously, as the hon. member knows, the position of this government is that our forces are there to support the UN Resolution, to insist on the enforcement of that resolution, and to bring about a peaceful resolution of the dispute in the gulf.
If there is any change in the role of our forces, the government obviously would have to take that into consideration and would certainly advise the members of the opposition parties as quickly as possible.

HUMAN RIGHTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister for External Relations. The minister knows that despite strong opposition from the African National Congress and despite very serious state violence in the black townships, the European Community yesterday lifted the ban on new investment in South Africa.
Will Canada maintain our ban on new investment in South Africa until there has been irreversible change in the policy of apartheid in South Africa as defined by the African National Congress and as defined by the South African Council of Churches?
[Translation\

Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend is well aware that these are multilateral sanctions which we approved within the framework of the Commonwealth. We are determined to maintain our present policy until the responsible ministers meet again in March of next year. My hon. friend is also well aware that the Government of Canada sincerely believes that the sanctions must be
December 17, 1990

maintained as long as there is no evidence of irreversible change in the policy of apartheid in South Africa. Such has always been and remains our position for the time being.

subtopic: HUMAN RIGHTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my supplementary question to the same minister also has to do with the issue of human rights in Africa.
In view of the serious violations of human rights in Zaire, including the killing of students, will the Government of Canada exert pressures so that the Francophone Summit be moved from Zaire, will cancel all assistance and credit to the government of that country and demand the immediate release of all the students currently in Zairian prisons, including Reverend Brother Victore Digekisa, President of the Student Union?

speakeroldname: Hon. Monique Landry (Minister for External Relations):
speakerposition: Minister for External Relations; Minister responsible for La Francophonie
subtopic: HUMAN RIGHTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend is certainly aware of this government's position concerning the human rights issue. Last week, I personally met the Zairian Minister of Foreign Affairs while on a visit to Canada and so did my colleague Marcel Masse. During our discussions, I conveyed to him the government's concern about the disregard for human rights and the democratic process which seems to be developing in Zaire.
My hon. friend referred to past events. Following the Lubumbashi massacres, I sent for the Zairian ambassador to express to him our very deep concern about these incidents. I had requested at the time that his government should authorize an international inquiry into the Lubumbashi events. We continue to give enornous significance to the human rights issue and the democratic process and we will take the every step necessary in this connection.

FORESTRY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of Forestry.
In its report entitled Forests of Canada-The Federal Role, the House of Commons subcommittee on forestry has recommended development of a national forest inventory and data base as a major priority in any strategy for sustainable forestry development in Canada. Such a system would entail not only perpetual statistical control of trees and timber, but also an integrated and constant analysis of wildlife, mineral deposits, ecological reserves, parklands and all other values of the forest, both economical and environmental.
My question to the minister is as follows: does he share the view of the report that such an integrated inventory system and data base is an essential priority for the future management of Canada's forestry resources and, if so, does he accept the recommendation that the federal government must provide the leadership to establish such a system in partnership with the provinces and other stakeholders?

speakerposition: Minister of Forestry
subtopic: FORESTRY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, not only can I tell my hon. friend that I support this kind of approach, but that we are well under way in co-operation with and under the control of the council of forest ministers in the country to update our data systems and put in place a national data system that would respect the principles that he has enunciated in

December 17, 1990
Oral Questions
his report, namely, the need for integrated management and the management of the timber and non-timber assets in our forests. I am pleased to be able to say to my friend that early in the new year, when I am required to make my first report to Parliament, some of these new statistics will be reflected.

AGRICULTURE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the price discovery mechanisms for grains in the marketplace are not working. Due to concentration in the corporate sector and various United States subsidy programs, such as their target prices and deficiency payments and the Export Enhancement Program, will the Acting Prime Minister assure the House today, before Christmas, that Canadian grain farmers will not have to carry the burden of these misguided United States actions and will be compensated with reasonable prices for their highest quality grain in the world?

speakeroldname: Hon. Pierre Blais (Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs and Minister of State (Agriculture)):
speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs; Minister of State (Agriculture)
subtopic: AGRICULTURE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the question raised by my colleague deals with the price of grains. You can see how right Canada is to defend, internationally and more particularly at the GATT, the position that the present grain war is nonsense. It is nonsense for Canada and for all countries closely interested.
We believe that if the Europeans could be convinced to water down their wine and display more flexibility, especially at this time-we did receive mildly optimistic reports from our representatives, as the members of this House did from the Standing Committees last week-it is likely that we could build on solid ground in the GATT negociations, starting in January. To support the Canadian farmers who produce high standard wheat, Mr. Speaker, we absolutely need to reach an agreement at the GATT negociations and I can assure you that Canada will not let this chance go by.

subtopic: AGRICULTURE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is interesting to note that some very prominent Canadian farm leaders marched with the European farmers in Brussels a couple of weeks ago showing support for the EEC position at GATT. Under the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement, the United States must take into account the impact that export subsidies have on Canada.
Will this government use the instruments provided for in this agreement to seek consultations and compensation for losses incurred by the Canadian Wheat Board and by the Canadian farmers for the 1990-91 crop year?

speakeroldname: Hon. Pierre Blais (Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs and Minister of State (Agriculture)):
speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs; Minister of State (Agriculture)
subtopic: AGRICULTURE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member ought to know that last year, the government had consultations with grain producers across Canada. We had a federal-provincial conference in November in Winnipeg, where we practically reached an agreement on a long-term program.
What Canadian grain producers need, in addition to a GATT agreement that will help them get a fair price on international markets, is a program that provides a safety net at the national level that will help them plan for the future. As far as consultation is concerned, Mr. Speaker, this Canadian government has consulted with farm producers more than any other government. We have nothing to be ashamed of in this respect.

subtopic: AGRICULTURE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my supplementary is to the same minister. Witnesses who have appeared before the Standing Committee on Health and Welfare for the past year have asked for adequate funding of community health care.
Will the minister commit to the House today that he will exercise more federal leadership and expand the mandate of the Canada Health Act to also include funding of community health care, as reflected in the report of the Standing Committee on Health and Welfare tabled in this House of Commons six months ago?

speakeroldname: Hon. Perrin Beatty (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: AGRICULTURE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Government of Canada has shown considerable leadership in the whole field of health.
We transfer to the provinces each year some $14 billion to assist them in the provision of health services. In addition to that, we have shown leadership in fighting against AIDS, in terms of the fight against tobacco, drug abuse, and a whole range of other issues which affect the health of Canadians.
One thing that we also do, however, is respect the Constitution of Canada. We respect the fact that the delivery of health care services is given to the provinces within the confines of the Canada Health Act. We believe that is an appropriate division of responsibilities.

GOODS AND SERVICES TAX
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Finance.
Now that the Senate has passed the GST, Quebec has already exempted books from this tax and the Prime Minister of Canada promised to consider this a few weeks ago, is the minister prepared to make a formal commitment today that he will amend the goods and
Oral Questions
services tax legislation to provide an exemption for books? Is the minister prepared to accept the fact that taxing books means imposing ignorance?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance
subtopic: GOODS AND SERVICES TAX
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member is wrong when he makes those comments.
We are not taxing educational services. We are not taxing public-If the hon. member says we are, he should read the legislation.
We are not taxing libraries. These are important elements in the whole battle against illiteracy in this country. My hon. friend realizes that we have not had Royal Assent. That, I expect, will come later today. We have said, with something as major as the goods and services tax legislation, that we will wait a period of time and review the impact that the GST has on various segments of the economy. After that, we will be in a better position to make some decisions.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, perhaps I could ask for leave, pursuant to Standing Order 52, for an emergency debate on the subject of the Persian Gulf and the situation there.
It arises out of the events of this past weekend. There had been planned meetings between the Secretary of State of the United States and the Foreign Minister of the Government of Iraq. Those meetings this past weekend have been cancelled, leading all observers of the grave situation in the Middle East to a new concern that war will break out in the Middle East shortly after January 15, the deadline established by the United Nations.
These events have added some urgency for this House because of the contemplated recess of the House in a few days. Given the deep concern of Canadians about the possible role of Canadian forces and the need for a commitment from the government before Canadian forces are committed to the situation in Iraq in any offensive capacity, this House must meet and must approve it. It is therefore, in my respectful submission, urgent that this House today deal with the situation as a

Government Orders
result of the weekend's events and have a debate on the issue of Canadian participation in offensive action in the gulf and a clear commitment from the government that there will be no such move by the government without clear parliamentary approval.

speechtext:
Motion No. 6A
That Bill C-84 be amended in Clause 9 by adding immediately
after line 26 at page 3 the following:
"(a) provisions insuring that the Governor in Council be entitled to appoint one director to the Board of Directors of Petro-Canada;"
He said: Mr. Speaker, this is yet another further attempt to see to it that there is some continuing public presence, some continuing reflection of the community and its concerns, as Petro-Canada makes its decisions.
After all, we have a company into which the Canadian people have put tremendous amounts of money. The total amount of taxpayers' money which has gone into this company is something like $4.3 billion in 1990

dollars. Inking inflation into account, that investment amounts to over $6.8 billion.
If we had a sense that this company would be sold for anything close to $6.8 billion and that money was going to come back to the people of Canada, then it might make some logical sense for the public authorities of this country to cut themselves off entirely from Petro-Cana-da. I still think it would be a serious mistake in terms of our national energy hopes for the future, but one could see the logic.
However, the minister indicated in testimony before committee that he simply did not know how much money would be received for the shares of this company. For instance, my colleague from Edmonton East asked him point blank: "What you are telling me is that the government does not really have a clue. The government simply does not know how much money it will get for the sale of Petro-Canada". I should congratulate the minister on his frankness when he responded by saying: "That is right. We do not know what we are going to get for the sale of Petro-Canada".
The minister was then asked by the hon. member for Edmonton East if there was a price below which the government would not go, but the minister would not name a price. He would not even say that it was the intention of the government to see to it that the taxpayers of this country would recoup the amount for which the company is valued on the books after some fairly slick accounting wizardry had recently reduced taxpayers' equity by $1.8 billion.
We have a company created by the taxpayers of Canada and expanded by the taxpayers of Canada. It was the recipient in present dollar terms of something like $6.8 billion in assistance and investment from the government, yet the government intends to cut its ties completely with this company.
What a total, absolute, abdication of responsibility to the taxpayers of the country, on the part of the future consumers of the country and on the part of the future people of the country who depend on this company for energy supplies.
We have suggested with this amendment that the government would be entitled to appoint one director to Petro-Canada's board, simply one director. We are not
Government Orders
talking about government control of that board. We are not talking about a great mass of government bureaucrats. We are talking about a single director, so that there would be a chance for the public interest to be represented in the decision making that takes place in this company.
That director could of course be out-voted. It would be possible for that director to face a situation where he or she puts the public interest first, as cabinet saw it, before the Petro-Canada board and Petro-Canada says no, that it intends to follow the dictates of its bottom line and to seek to make decisions on the basis of what is most profitable for it, and that it is not going to listen.
This is not a suggestion that the director appointed by cabinet would have any extra power or authority, but that director would have the capacity to do two things: first, to convey to Petro-Canada, this company that we as taxpayers have put so much money into, the concerns of the public as reflected through the government of the day and, second, to be through participation on the Petro-Canada board, if not a window on the industry, at least a little peephole or a little chance for the government to have some direct insight into what is taking place with respect to this particular industry.
This is an industry which is crucial to the future of our country. It is crucial for the future of consumers and for the future of manufacturers. It is crucial for the future of resource producers in every part of the country that have to make use of gasoline or motor oil. Yet, if this amendment is not accepted, there will simply be a complete cut between the government which established this company and the company itself. This is not something remarkable or unusual. In many cases of privatization throughout the world, government has maintained the power to appoint at least one director. That director has proved an important communications link between the company and the government, subject of course to rules of confidentiality.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subtopic: PETRO-CANADA PUBLIC PARTICIPATION ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
As a new candidate I felt it was my obligation in preparing to run for election and hopefully to be a member of this place, to spend some of that time in preparation, learning about pieces of public policy that I felt I was not comfortable with, that I did not know enough about.
Certainly in my case, as someone who was raised primarily in the city, agriculture was one of those areas and I spent many hours at it.
But the other was the oil industry. I was bom in Calgary and grew up there. Many of my friends and acquaintances worked in one facet or another of the oil industry. Yet when facing the possibility of coming here as a member of Parliament I realized how little I really knew about it and how great the need was to learn more about it. I set about doing that. It would certainly have been easier for me in the city of Calgary than it might have been for members in other communities such as Windsor, to really be able to get people voluntarily to teach me about this industry because Calgary is the capital and Calgary is the centre.
One of the people who was my mentor was a man who was the president and the chairman of the board of a company called Voyageur Petroleum. When we became the government in 1979, he headed a committee on behalf of the government to look into the divestiture of Petro-Canada. They brought forward a report in December of that year which never became public policy because we subsequently lost the vote in the House of Commons and we lost an election.
Why did we, in 1979, and why did I, in the intervening time from December 3,1977 until running for election in 1979, become so convinced and so persuaded that it was a piece of very bad public policy to create Petro-Canada in the first place, and that it was an even worse piece of

public policy to maintain it over all these intervening years.
I have read and listened to speeches that come from the other side. I say to members opposite, by and large, you do not know what you are talking about. You have no sense of reality about the funding and the financing of this corporation and what it did to our nation. It was an ideological decision to create this company in the first place. The cost of it was horrendous.
Prior to my running for office, Petro-Canada had acquired its first two smaller oil companies. The public treasury lost its income tax contribution because the minute they came into Petro-Canada's hands, they had no profit. In fact, the grants that the public, all of a sudden, had to give to those companies exceeded the income tax that it had been getting.
When I listen to the member opposite talk about all of the public money invested in this corporation. We had given up essentially, 15 years of income tax. We know how that compounds in the system and the contribution it would have made to deficit reduction over that entire 15-year period of time. We compounded the problem by giving them until 1984, until we became the government, annual grants of substantial size over and above those that were available to the industry generally, just for this corporation specifically.
In the entire period of time from the creation of this corporation until today, the government has had to borrow money to meet its operating expenses, that is, until the last three years when we have a little bit of money to apply the interest on the public debt.
We are talking about governments that went into the private sector, destroyed private companies by bringing them into Petro-Canada and paying for them with borrowed dollars. Canadians are stuck paying the interest on that public debt. My friend is worried about getting $4 billion back from Petro-Canada when it is worth over $7 billion. I heard him earlier in Question Period saying, "restore the money to the CBC. Give them the $108 million that they are asking for". Give, give, give. If we had even $4 billion, let alone $7.8 billion, would we not having to pay interest on it because it was a reduction of the public debt, $4 billion at 10 per cent, which is below market rates, is $400 million. We could give the CBC four times what it is asking for if that is his
Government Orders
priority. But no, he would rather own comer service stations, asphalt, gas tank hoses and little numbers that run up and down. I am talking about the New Democrat who put these motions and just spoke, but it is a speech I have heard from the Liberals a thousand times.
I will tell you what it did to my city. When the government decided, for ideological reasons, that it had to move in this direction, it distorted, almost overnight, the entire labour market of an industry in the upward direction by about 35 per cent. It made all the costs for every oil company in this country on the staffing side at least 30 per cent to 35 per cent higher almost overnight and was a root cause of the runaway inflation in the early 1980s. This was the root cause of a whole lot of suicides and spousal batterings and this kind of stuff, because the government had blinders and said: "We must be involved in the oil industry at any cost and at any price". What advice did it give us? It did this under the rubric that it had this superlative advice that would put the Government of Canada in a position to do something, but what it was in a position to do was to inflate prices.

As the sale goes on, as we piece off more and more of Petro-Canada, we approach what we could call the grey line-it is not a red line, it is a grey line-where we are not sure whether the big block shareholder has control or not. In some widely-held corporations the control block can involve as little as 10 or 15 per cent of the shares outstanding. So what do we do, the people of Canada, when our government holds, something in the vicinity of 10 or 15 per cent, let us say, of the outstanding shares of Petro-Canada? We have one foot on the dock and one foot on the boat and we may find we no longer have control. We have an interest but we no longer have any representation on the board. This amendment would ensure that the Governor in Council had that right to appoint at least one person to the board.
The amendment, as it is structured, would run past the total divestiture date. It would go on forever. It would be in perpetuity, I suppose, as long as Petro-Canada was around. Given the origins of Petro-Canada I cannot say that would be a bad thing for us or for Petro-Canada.

What I say to the New Democratic Party is that if that is what it wants to do with stations around the country-and there are many people who have set up businesses to collect old oil and recycle it and are doing a fine job at it-you cannot just take one corporation in a competitive environment, as the hon. member mentioned, one that is competing with other companies and place the onus on that company which places it at a disadvantage to other competitors. If you do that, and place an environmental stipulation on an industry, then do it as a whole so it is competitive for all of them. But do not place one corporation in an uncompetitive position. on a fair and equitable basis and speaks to the environment as a whole and does not place the onus on one or two Canadian companies.

It wants to place a Canadian company in unfair competition with foreign interests in this country. That is hogwash.
The other interesting thing about this is that they are asking us to place an onus on a Canadian company when they are not placing it on the foreign companies. That is exactly what they want to do.
