Motion No. 15
That Bill C-84 be amended in clause 9 by striking out line 29 at
page 4 and substituting the following therefor.
"(e) financing of Petro-Canada or for so long as the Minister holds any voting shares of Petro-Canada, from disposing of any asset of Petro-Canada which the Minister has designated in writing as a strategic asset, where the Minister has published notice of same in The Canada Gazette prior to the completion of any such disposition."
He said: Mr. Speaker, this proposed amendment respecting the bill privatizing Petro-Canada deals with an issue that arose during the debate, the discussions and the hearing of witnesses at committee. It derives from a projection into the future of certain fact se-
Govemment Orders
quences which might prove to be a problem for Petro-Canada, for the government, and for the shareholders.
The proposed amendment sets out that the minister- and that would be the minister designated under this particular bill-would have the opportunity to prevent a sale by Petro-Canada of an asset described as a strategic asset.
Why is that important to us? If we look at the reason for having a state oil company in the first place, we see we can define certain national interests that require us to act or take steps as a country and as a nation. In this case the state oil company would take steps on behalf of all of us to protect our vital interests in areas deemed to be of strategic importance.
When I talk about strategic importance or strategic assets or vital interests, I am talking about economic areas of activity engaged in now by Petro-Canada, areas where Canadians and the government have wanted Petro-Canada to be active from the beginning, exploration for domestic oil reserves and distribution of energy commodities in this country.
The difficulty we see arising is one in a future that would not be quite so orderly and planned as what we like to think would mature in the ordinary course. I am talking about a situation that would evolve in the economy and politically around the world. I suppose the current gulf crisis is an example. Although that particular crisis is quite a way offshore, it has affected us here in Canada. It has affected our oil price.
However, in this unseen future I think what I am looking at is a change in circumstances whereupon the people of Canada, from all across the country or from a particular region, would say to this government that in acting for all of us it must take a step in our interest to protect us or to foster the national interest in a particular field of the economy.
I am talking about, for example, maintaining in business a refinery that is strategically located in our national interest in a particular region, in a particular area. I am talking about the sale of particular reserves of crude, and even of a particular type of crude, in a particular area of the country where it would be seen to be in our national interest for that crude not to fall into foreign hands or offshore control. I am also talking about the sale, conveyance or even abandonment of transportation infrastructure by Petro-Canada, which by that point in time will be our former state oil company. We will either still have a percentage interest or even a large interest, but because of the process of divestiture and privatiza-

December 17, 1990
Government Orders
tion we will have given up administrative or, practically speaking any role in the running of the company and the decisions it would be making.
As well I am talking about the sale of a pipeline, the abandonment of a pipeline. I noted last week or two weeks ago a projection that the pipeline which runs from southern Ontario to Montreal could be shut down by 1991. Petro-Canada does not have anything to do with that pipeline. However, I am talking about a situation wherein the government is called upon by the electorate to intervene, protect, and stabilize an enterprise like a pipeline to ensure that the people of Montreal, for example, have access to western Canadian crude. I have referred to the refinery, the reserves, the transportation, the infrastructure, and the pipeline. There are perhaps other unforeseen areas where Canadians will demand that their government intervene, protect and stabilize a particular strategic asset.
By placing this amendment in this bill, it will provide notice to Petro-Canada, to its competitors, and to its new shareholders that Canadians still retain the right to intervene if they feel it is in their national interest to do so.
I know that does not sit well in the private sector. I know that a provision like this one will affect to some degree the price of shares, but in the phase of moving from no privately held shares to all privately held shares we have to go through the process where the potential purchaser of shares knows very well that the people of Canada still have an interest in Petro-Canada. Whether that process takes five years or ten years, it is still going to be there for us.
There is no need in this amendment to define what is a strategic asset. Some people may ask: "How can you provide for a right for the minister to force Petro-Canada to retain a strategic asset when you have not defined what it is?" I would maintain that when the minister is called upon to act, he or she would know exactly what that asset was. As long as the government felt that it was an asset disposition which required its intervention, that
would be a sufficient reason for intervening. I am sure that that intervention would not be taken lightly.
The amendment provides that notice of same would be published in The Canada Gazette. I am sure as well that there might be offers to the government: "If you are going to prevent us from disposing of it, then perhaps you ought to expropriate it". I do not know whether or not we will get into that kind of situation. It would place us right back to where we were when Petro-Canada was created in the first place, where there was a perceived need for a national oil company that had the means of participating in the marketplace and in the upstream and downstream side. When Petro-Canada was created of course it was the upstream side that was targeted, but it is that national interest the people will wish us to pursue.
That is the reason for the amendment. I believe it fairly describes the situation wherein such intervention would have to be involved, at least in terms of process. I hope the House will support my amendment.

Mr. Speaker, I listened to that last speech by the hon. member of the socialist party. Once Petro-Canada ceases to be wholly owned by the Crown, it's business activities fall under provincial jurisdiction. That is the difference between an oil company and an airline company.
When Air Canada was privatized, it still was under federal jurisdiction. When Petro-Canada is privatized, it will come under provincial jurisdiction, just like its competitors.
Parliament has really no constitutional basis to legislate a privatized Petro-Canada directly in respect of language. Application of even a part of the Official Languages Act to a privatized Petro-Canada would put
the federal government in the untenable position of regulating an activity over which it has no jurisdiction. That causes us some problems.
The only way it could do this is to specifically override provincial jurisdiction in the manner suggested by Motion No. 23.1 am not sure that my hon. friend wants that. I know what he wants. rial governments in this regard. Therefore, we feel that the bill as it stands covers the area of official languages.

Knowing that the hon. member does not speak French, I can only hope that he will understand what I am about to say in that language.
The declaratory power is what enables the Parliament of Canada, under section 92(10(c), to change proprio moto, without consent and at the expense of the provincial legislative powers, the exclusive jurisdiction of the provinces over the local works it has declared to be for the general advantage of Canada or for the advantage of two or more of the provinces.
Incidentally, paragraphs (b) and (d) deal with the nature of this power. It is a special power.

December 17, 1990
Government Orders

If one believes in Canada, there are certain areas where one makes priorities, choices, and options.

Although this a special power, Parliament used it extensively, as Mrs. Andree Lajoie explained in her remarkable book on the subject. She wrote: "Parliament specifically declared to be for the general advantage the dams, canals, battlefields, railways, companies, grain elevators, landings stages, gas pipelines, slides, a piece of legislation, a subway, an oil pipeline, bridges-including several international bridges-trenches and tunnels."
Is is often argued that, and I quote: "The business or company is declared to be for the general advantage of Canada". We will examine the validity of this line in a moment. This line was used to exercice declaratory power regarding the following works, and I quote: "Company shares, harbour improvements, aqueducts, aircraft, buses, benches, basins, drydocks, water falls, docks, motor power, electricity, warehouses, companies involved in lumber, home building, railways, breeding, messengers, transport, terminals, garages, harbours, hotels, mines, mills, ships, works and undertakings-and on and on-of the federal district and later of the region of the national capital, oil refineries, restaurants, saw mills, telegraphs, underwater cables, telephones, theaters, tramways-of Montreal, Quebec, Ottawa and elsewhere-steel mills, brick factories, steel plants, pulp and paper mills, chemical plants, precious metal and gold refineries. Government should be involved in regulating and making priorities for the long-term benefit of society. Today, unfortunately, instead we see government doing what it does best, trying to do everything else. Where has that gotten us, Mr. Speaker? When we are looking at the whole idea of this motion about what is best for Canada, what would be for our advantage, unfortunately what we have seen is that instead of the government ensuring that Canada's future is economically sound, many in Canada are concerned with maintaining the institutions of the past whether or not they have been contributors to the Canadian economy and society.

The public can rightly be confused. The politicians are confused over this issue as well. This despite the fact that the government may find its private sector industry generally profitable and willing to compete without the government being one of the participants.
The taxpaying public may well ask whether there is a cheaper way to regulate an industry than by owning a company, which invariably becomes a political toy, a place to put old supporters as well paid directors and encouraging policy decisions that are politically expedient but perhaps not economically sound.

Mr. Speaker, I want to thank my hon. friend for giving me a couple of minutes before we vote on these amendments.
We will have covered all the amendments that were brought forward by the opposition party.
First of all let me comment for a moment on the disclosure of information motion. Securities legislation across this country requires a company to issue a prospectus whenever it issues shares to the public. The regulations governing the contents of a prospectus require it to disclose the proceeds and the cost of the issue. It must all be there before it is permitted to go forward.
Funds received by the sale of Petro-Canada, the shares, will be reported in the public accounts which are tabled in Parliament. As we know, we have a debt of $4.3 billion on our books that has to be written off.

December 17, 1990

Of course the minister will continue to disclose to the Auditor General information that he is required by law to disclose in connection with the Public Accounts of Canada. Those are all covered. So this amendment No. 20 is not necessary.
As far as amendment No. 32 is concerned, the information to be tabled in this proposed report that they are talking about is available from other sources that are required under other existing laws, so inclusion of this provision is redundant and unnecessary.
Security legislation requires a company to issue a prospectus whenever it issues shares to the public. That is well known. When privatization takes place, Petro-Canada will become a widely-held public company subject to all the requirements of a public company. We, of course, will report where the income goes from Petro-Canada as these shares are sold off. Both these motions are totally unnecessary and we will be voting against them.
